title: Famine, the Gibeonites, and Rizpah's Vigil
summary: A three-year famine leads David to seek the LORD, who names its cause: Saul's slaughter of the Gibeonites in violation of Israel's ancient oath to them. At the Gibeonites' demand, David hands over seven of Saul's descendants, who are executed at Gibeah, and Saul's concubine Rizpah guards their bodies for months until David gives them, with the bones of Saul and Jonathan, an honorable burial. The chapter ends with four brief battle reports in which David's men kill Philistine giants descended from Rapha.
story: Chapters 21 through 24 of 2 Samuel form an appendix to David's story. They are not in chronological order; they gather episodes, lists, and poems from across his reign and arrange them with care. This chapter reaches back into the past. Saul has been dead for years, but a wrong he did still lies on the land. The story shows that God's covenant promises bind across generations, even promises made to foreigners, and that David, now firmly king, must deal with the unfinished business of Saul's house. It also brings Saul's story to a quiet close: the bones of the first king and his son Jonathan finally rest in the family tomb in Benjamin. The giant-slaying reports that follow recall David's own victory over Goliath and show that the battles he once fought alone are now fought by his servants.
historical:
The famine episode probably belongs to the early or middle part of David's reign, sometime after he took Mephibosheth into his household (chapter 9), since verse 7 assumes that arrangement. The Gibeonites lived in a cluster of towns north of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin. Joshua 9 tells how they tricked Joshua into swearing a treaty of peace with them in the LORD's name, and Israel kept that oath even after discovering the deception. Saul's attempt to wipe them out is not narrated anywhere else; this chapter is our only source, and it explains his motive as zeal for Israel and Judah, perhaps a nationalist drive to clear non-Israelites out of Benjamin, his home tribe.

The victims come from two women. Rizpah, Saul's concubine, appeared earlier when Abner slept with her (3:7). The mother of the other five is given as Merab in the BSB, following some Hebrew and Greek manuscripts; most Hebrew manuscripts read Michal, but Merab was the daughter of Saul who married Adriel the Meholathite (1 Samuel 18:19), so many translations adopt her name here. The giants are called descendants of Rapha, linked with the Rephaim, a people remembered in Israel as tall and formidable (Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 20-21).
cultural:
Ancient Israel took oaths sworn in the LORD's name with great seriousness. Breaking one invited divine judgment, and the land itself could suffer for bloodshed that was not answered (Numbers 35:33 says blood pollutes the land). In the ancient Near East, famine was widely read as a sign of divine displeasure, and David does what a king should: he seeks the face of the LORD. The Gibeonites refuse money, which could have been paid as compensation in some cases, and ask instead for a life-for-life settlement from the house of the man who tried to exterminate them. The execution takes place at Gibeah, Saul's own town, and the bodies are exposed as a public sign.

In that world, leaving a body unburied and exposed to birds and animals was the worst dishonor that could be done to the dead. Rizpah's vigil, lasting from the barley harvest in spring until the autumn rains, is a mother's defiant act of love and protest. She spreads sackcloth, the rough cloth of mourning, and keeps watch day and night. Her faithfulness moves David to act, and proper burial in the ancestral tomb restores dignity to Saul's family.
literary: The chapter has two unequal parts. The first (verses 1-14) is a tightly told narrative that begins with famine and ends with the land healed: God answered their prayers for the land, the chapter's resolution. Rizpah's vigil sits at the turning point, and the story moves from judgment to honor once David hears of her. The second part (verses 15-22) is a list of four short battle notes, each built on the same pattern (another battle, a named hero, a slain descendant of Rapha), ending with a summary in verse 22. Verse 19 is famous as a textual puzzle. The Hebrew says Elhanan killed Goliath the Gittite; 1 Chronicles 20:5 says he killed Lahmi, Goliath's brother. The BSB supplies the brother of from Chronicles. Some scholars think the Samuel text has suffered a copying error; others think Goliath's fame drew his name into a separate tradition. The appendix as a whole is arranged symmetrically, and this chapter pairs with chapter 24: both open with a national disaster tied to a king's sin, and both end with God answering prayer for the land.

outline.t: Famine and its cause: Saul's crime against the Gibeonites
The Gibeonites' demand and the execution of Saul's seven descendants
Rizpah's vigil and the burial of Saul's house
Three more giants fall to David's men

doctrines.note: An oath sworn in the LORD's name centuries earlier, even to a people who deceived Israel to get it, still binds. God holds his people to their word, and breaking faith with outsiders is breaking faith with him.

Bloodguilt left unaddressed brings consequences on the land. The chapter is uncomfortable, but it insists that injustice to the vulnerable is not forgotten by God simply because time has passed or a king has died.
David seeks the LORD when the famine persists, and the chapter closes with God answering prayer for the land. Prayer here is part of how a king leads a suffering people.

words.note: Kipper, to atone or make amends, the same verb used for the priestly sacrifices of Leviticus. David asks the Gibeonites how he can make atonement so that they will bless the LORD's inheritance. Here it means to cover or settle a wrong so that relationship is restored, and it shows how seriously the offense was taken.

Shevuah, oath. Verse 7 turns on it: David spares Mephibosheth because of the oath between David and Jonathan. The whole chapter is about oaths, Israel's to the Gibeonites and David's to Jonathan, and about keeping one's word before the LORD.

Ner, lamp. David's men call him the lamp of Israel (verse 17), the light whose going out would leave the nation in darkness. The image returns in 1 Kings, where God keeps a lamp for David in Jerusalem, a picture of the dynasty's survival under God's promise (1 Kings 11:36).

christ: The link to Christ here is thematic rather than predictive. The chapter shows sin whose consequences fall on descendants and a settlement reached through the deaths of others, and it leaves readers troubled, as it should. The law itself forbade putting children to death for the sins of their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16), and the prophets later insisted that each person answers for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:20). The New Testament presents Jesus' death as a different kind of settlement: not the forced death of innocent descendants demanded by the wronged, but the willing self-giving of the one who carries the guilt of others (1 Peter 3:18). And David's men call their king the lamp of Israel; John's Gospel speaks of Jesus as the light that darkness has not overcome (John 1:5).

hard.q: How could God allow seven of Saul's descendants to die for Saul's crime?
hard.a: This is one of the hardest passages in the historical books, and it should be read with its difficulty intact. The text says the LORD named the cause of the famine, but it does not say that the LORD commanded the execution; the Gibeonites asked for it and David agreed. Some interpreters therefore read the settlement as a human response within the customs of the time, one the narrator reports without endorsing every part of it, and they point to Deuteronomy 24:16, which forbids executing children for their fathers' sins. Others argue that Saul's household was implicated in the massacre (verse 1 speaks of Saul and his family), so the executed men may not have been simply innocent. Still others note that the ancient world thought of guilt more corporately than modern readers do, and that the land was only healed after the burial, not immediately after the executions. What the chapter plainly does is honor Rizpah, whose grief and fidelity move the king, and it leaves the reader unsettled about the cost of broken covenants.

questions: A promise made long ago, to people Israel did not want to keep faith with, still mattered to God. What commitments are you tempted to treat as expired?
Rizpah could not stop the executions, but she refused to let the dead be dishonored. What can faithful love do when it cannot change an outcome?
David's men told him he could no longer go into battle. When have you needed others to protect you from your own limits?
